newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarians call hotline with reform proposals.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarians call hotline with reform proposals.

text.p: Up to 100 Bulgarians a day are calling a "telephone of change" hotline to offer suggestions on anything from the country's banking crisis to the need for a free rock concert.

The line was set up at the election campaign headquarters of the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) at the suggestion of Sofia university students who were the backbone of daily street protests which toppled the Socialist government in February.
"We are keeping a record of all calls, even those which are obviously not sensible," said political science student Nikolai Hranov, adding that they were logging 50 to 100 calls a day.
People from all over Bulgaria are calling in to share their concerns on social security, the progress of economic reforms or the soaring prices of medicines and food.

"The people are fed up with the ignorance of the people in power and they appreciate this type of communication," Hranov said. "Most of them want transparency on the activities of the cabinet and they want the telephone of change to stay in operation even after the elections."

One of the accusations levelled against the former Socialist government was its secrecy. Interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski has made frequent media appearances to explain the reform programme and many callers to the "telephone of change" want to share thoughts on the economic crisis.

"The legal amendments referring to foreign investments are not adequate and should be updated," said Dimitar Novoselski, while Petar Angelov contributed: "We have to deal immediately with environmental problems".

Some of the calls are directly connected to the campaign for April 19 elections, including one which suggested the UDF, tipped to form the next government, could attract more votes by raising pensions.

"I am looking forward to the coming elections because I am 74 years old and before I die I want to see that my children and grandchildren will have a chance for a better life than mine," Margarita Georgieva said.

Another caller said state institutions should appoint young, attractive spokespeople to improve their image, while Stefan Shopov wanted food coupons distributed to the poorest Bulgarians and Nikolai Georgiev suggested getting rid of big, communist-era industrial projects.
"We need to go back to the old economic structures and we can start by closing down the Kozloduy nuclear power plant and the Kremikovtsi steelworks," he said.
"It is true that some of the calls are strange, even absurd, but anyway we are keeping a record of everything and all calls are sorted and discussed by the UDF media council," Hranov said.
Surprisingly few calls are abusive, but not all are completely serious.

"Nothing has been done for the young people who helped the UDF to topple the Socialist cabinet, so why don't you organise a free rock concert, something like Deep Purple or Aerosmith maybe," Miladin Manov said.
